stories.bridge: This is the company behind your assessment — know its story cold, because the interview will test whether you understand what it sells and why it matters. Let's learn ThreatLocker in sixty seconds, then earn the depth.
stories.hook: In 2017, in Orlando, Florida, an ethical hacker who had watched ransomware nearly destroy a client's business decided the industry had it backwards.
stories.narrative: Danny Jenkins had spent two decades in IT and cybersecurity — red team, blue team, the full circuit — and he'd reached a conclusion that became the company's founding thesis: the industry was trying to recognize bad software, and losing. Every antivirus, every detection engine, was a bet that you could enumerate evil faster than attackers could invent it. Jenkins's inversion: stop trying to recognize bad. Decide what's good — allowlist it — and block everything else by default. He founded ThreatLocker in 2017 in Orlando with Sami Jenkins (COO) and John Carolan, building a Zero Trust endpoint platform around that deny-by-default core: Application Allowlisting (only approved software runs), Ringfencing (even approved apps get their permissions tightly scoped, so a compromised browser can't launch PowerShell), plus Storage Control, Elevation Control, and Network Control. The human side became a differentiator too: Cyber Hero, the company's 24/7/365 support team, answers in about a minute — a deliberate contrast with an industry where 'support' means a ticket queue. The company grew fast on the strength of the model: thousands of organizations, millions of endpoints, major funding rounds, and a headquarters in Maitland, Florida. For your assessment, the story matters because it explains the product logic you'll be tested on: every triage decision — approve, deny, ringfence — flows from the founding inversion. Don't memorize features; understand the bet. The industry tries to recognize bad. ThreatLocker decided to define good. The Cyber Hero model is the operational expression of the founding bet: if you block by default, customers need fast, expert humans to approve the legitimate exceptions — so support becomes part of the product, not a cost center. For your assessment, internalize the triage logic the story implies: default-deny first, allowlist deliberately, ringfence what you allow. The company's history is the answer key to its interview.
stories.title: The story behind ThreatLocker
verifiedClaims: ThreatLocker was founded in 2017 in Orlando by Danny Jenkins, Sami Jenkins, and John Carolan
Its platform is built on deny-by-default application allowlisting plus Ringfencing
Cyber Hero is its 24/7/365 support operation

stories.bridge: 1975 wrote the principles; ThreatLocker productized them. Now let's learn default-deny operations — from Learning Mode to least privilege — as engineering.

figures.name: Jerome Saltzer
figures.role: MIT researcher; co-author of the 1975 protection paper

stories.hook: In July 1975, two MIT researchers published the paper that predicted zero trust — nearly fifty years early.
stories.narrative: Jerome Saltzer and Michael Schroeder's 'The Protection of Information in Computer Systems,' published in the Communications of the ACM in July 1975, is the most quietly influential security paper ever written. In it they laid down eight design principles that read like a prophecy of everything this CBT teaches: least privilege (every subject gets only the access it needs), fail-safe defaults (access decisions default to denial), economy of mechanism (keep the security design small and simple), complete mediation, open design, separation of privilege, least common mechanism, and psychological acceptability. 'Fail-safe defaults' is deny-by-default in 1975 language: if the policy doesn't explicitly allow it, it's blocked. 'Least privilege' is Ringfencing's ancestor: even legitimate software gets only the permissions its job requires. The paper was written for the mainframe and minicomputer era, but its principles survived every platform shift because they're about the logic of protection, not the technology. When ThreatLocker's allowlisting blocks an unapproved executable, that's fail-safe defaults executing. When Ringfencing stops a compromised browser from launching a script interpreter, that's least privilege and economy of mechanism working. The assessment will test whether you can apply these principles under pressure — Learning Mode to baseline, policies to enforce, ringfencing to contain. Remember 1975 when you triage: the principles are fifty years old, the attackers are new, and the defaults are still the whole game. The 1975 paper's eighth principle — psychological acceptability — is the one practitioners forget and users pay for: security that fights its users gets bypassed. ThreatLocker's Learning Mode is the modern answer, baselining the legitimate before enforcing the deny. In this CBT you'll practice the full cycle: observe, baseline, enforce, contain. Saltzer and Schroeder wrote the principles; your triage decisions are the implementation. Observe, baseline, enforce, contain — the 1975 principles, operationalized for your triage shift.  Carry the eight principles into every shift.
stories.title: The story behind default-deny
verifiedClaims: Saltzer and Schroeder's paper was published in CACM, July 1975
It defined eight principles including least privilege and fail-safe defaults
The principles underlie modern allowlisting and zero trust

stories.bridge: The kill chain gave defenders the attacker's grammar; the attack graph gives you the map. Now let's learn to think in nodes and edges — the way the adversary moves.

figures.name: Eric Hutchins
figures.role: Lockheed Martin; co-author of the kill chain paper

figures.name: Michael Cloppert
figures.role: Lockheed Martin; co-author of the kill chain paper

figures.name: Rohan Amin
figures.role: Lockheed Martin; co-author of the kill chain paper

stories.hook: In 2011, three Lockheed Martin analysts gave defenders a grammar for the attack: seven phases, in order.
stories.narrative: Eric Hutchins, Michael Cloppert, and Rohan Amin worked on Lockheed Martin's computer incident response team, defending a prime defense contractor against state-sponsored intrusions. In their 2011 paper 'Intelligence-Driven Computer Network Defense Involving Adversary Campaigns and Kill Chain,' they proposed modeling every intrusion as a chain of seven phases: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives. The power was in the implication: the defender only needs to break one link to defeat the whole chain, so defense becomes about understanding where you can interdict. The model — adapted from the military's kill chain (find, fix, track, target, engage, assess) — gave the industry its first common language for describing campaigns, and it stuck. But practitioners soon found the limitation: real attacks aren't linear. Attackers loop back, skip phases, and branch — which is why the field evolved toward attack graphs, the nodes-and-edges model you'll master in this CBT. MITRE's ATT&CK framework (2013) then supplied the detailed vocabulary of tactics and techniques. Think of it as three generations: the kill chain gave us the phases, the attack graph gave us the map, ATT&CK gave us the street names. When you analyze an intrusion in the assessment, run all three: where in the chain are they, what does the graph of their possible moves look like, and which techniques are they using? The 2011 paper is the grammar; you're learning to write sentences. The model's military origin is worth remembering: it adapts the targeting cycle (find, fix, track, target, engage, assess) to network defense — the defender's kill chain breaks the attacker's. Its limitation taught the field the next lesson: real intrusions loop and branch, which is why your attack-graph module exists. Use the chain for the narrative, the graph for the analysis, ATT&CK for the vocabulary. Grammar, map, vocabulary — learn all three, and you'll read any intrusion.
stories.title: The story behind the kill chain
verifiedClaims: The Lockheed Martin kill chain paper was published in 2011
It defines seven phases from reconnaissance to actions on objectives
ATT&CK followed in 2013 as the technique-level vocabulary

stories.bridge: Bayes' theorem is the mathematics under your detection metrics — precision, recall, and why base rates rule everything. Now let's learn it properly, from 1763.

figures.name: Thomas Bayes
figures.role: Presbyterian minister; author of the 1763 essay

figures.name: Pierre-Simon Laplace
figures.role: Generalized Bayes' work into Bayesian inference

stories.hook: In 1763, the Royal Society of London read a paper by a minister who had been dead two years — and statistics changed forever.
stories.narrative: Thomas Bayes was a Presbyterian minister and amateur mathematician who never published his most important idea. After his death in 1761, his friend Richard Price found the manuscript and read it to the Royal Society in 1763; it appeared in the Philosophical Transactions as 'An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances.' The essay solved, in essence, the inverse problem: given that something happened, how should you update your belief about its cause? The theorem — posterior equals likelihood times prior, divided by the evidence — is the mathematics of changing your mind correctly. Pierre-Simon Laplace independently developed and generalized it, and for a century Bayesian reasoning was mainstream. Then came the long eclipse: the frequentists (Fisher, Neyman) dominated the twentieth century, and Bayes was dismissed as subjective — until the computers arrived. Bayesian methods came roaring back through the side door: spam filters (Paul Graham's 2002 'A Plan for Spam' made Bayesian filtering famous), machine learning, and eventually the detection engineering you'll practice. The base-rate lesson is the one this CBT needs you to feel in your bones: even a 99%-accurate detector is useless if the thing it detects is rare enough — the false positives drown the signal. Bayes' 1763 essay is why. When you compute precision and recall in the assessment, you're doing what Price read to the Royal Society: updating beliefs with evidence, correctly, two hundred sixty years later. Price, who read the paper, was himself remarkable — a minister, a mathematician, and the intellectual godfather of American independence through his pamphlets. The theorem's modern revenge is total: spam filters, medical diagnosis, machine learning, and your detection metrics all run on 1763. In the assessment, when you weigh an alert, you're Price's reader: updating beliefs with evidence, against the base rate, correctly. Update against the base rate, correctly, every time — that's the whole discipline.
stories.title: The story behind Bayes' theorem
verifiedClaims: Bayes' essay was read to the Royal Society in 1763 and published in the Philosophical Transactions
Laplace generalized the work into Bayesian inference
Bayesian spam filtering revived the method (Graham, 2002)
